title: Working Literacy Back Into the Secondary Classroom
author: Our Essential Story
summary: Writing as a literacy coach reflecting on a multi-year, whole-school literacy initiative, the author argues that the biggest determinant of whether such an effort spreads and lasts is not the curriculum chosen but the composition and pacing of the leadership team driving it. The central mistake she identifies in her own past work was building the leadership team almost entirely from ELA teachers, which unintentionally signaled that literacy remained an English-department responsibility rather than a schoolwide one. A second mistake was training only the literacy coach and a handful of administrators rather than the full interdisciplinary team, and launching before that team had itself been trained — leaving staff to sense that leadership was 'building the plane while flying it.' Her proposed redesign slows everything down: one instructional focus (vocabulary, then discussion, then text engagement, then text sets) added per year across a multi-year sequence, rather than cramming three courses into each cohort's single active year. The piece closes with a practical checklist for schools just starting this work.
points: An interdisciplinary leadership team, not an ELA-only one, is what actually signals literacy is a whole-school responsibility rather than an English-department project.
Train the full leadership team before launching to staff — launching before leaders understand the sequence reads to teachers as an unclear, scattered initiative.
Spreading one instructional focus per year (vocabulary, then discussion, then text engagement, then text sets) builds shared schoolwide language better than cramming three courses into a single year.
Administrators need explicit 'look-fors' tied to each year's focus so their observations and feedback stay aligned with what teachers are actually practicing.
Secondary teachers don't need to become elementary reading specialists — the goal is restoring reading, discussion, and meaning-making within each discipline's own content.
quotes: Literacy initiatives cannot thrive if they are only birthed from a district office, a consultant's slide deck, or one coach's calendar. The work needs local leadership from people who understand the culture, the schedule, the personalities, and the actual students in the building.

When an initiative is built mostly by ELA teachers, even with the best intentions, it can unintentionally communicate that literacy is still an English department project. When the work is shaped by disciplinary specialists across the building, it communicates that every content area has texts, language, questions, conversations, and ways of making meaning that students deserve access to.

The organization we partnered with offered a month-long training for literacy leaders. We chose to send the literacy coach, one administrator from each school, and a representative from special education. If I could do it again, I would train the entire literacy team.

Teachers can feel the difference between an initiative that has a thoughtful path and one that is being built while they are walking on it. When the adults leading the work are still trying to understand where it is going, the rest of the staff often experiences the initiative as unclear or scattered.
If I could change one major piece of the plan, I would spread the courses across the three years instead of having each cohort complete all three courses in a single year.

Slow initiatives give teachers time to understand the purpose behind the strategies. It lets departments adapt the work to their disciplines instead of performing generic literacy activities that feel disconnected from content. It allows administrators to learn what to look for and how to give feedback.
